title: Does your brain decide before you do?

lines.text: Your brain might decide to move before you do.
In 1983, Benjamin Libet asked people to flick their wrist whenever they felt like it, while watching a fast clock.
They reported the moment they felt the urge.
Brain activity linked to the movement started about half a second before it.

visual.label: ms before the move: brain activity

lines.text: But people only felt the urge about 200 milliseconds before.

visual.label: ms before: you feel the urge

lines.text: So the brain seemed to start roughly 300 milliseconds before the person was aware of choosing.
Libet himself thought we could still veto the action at the last moment.
And later research argued that signal might just be random brain noise, not a hidden decision.
So do you make your choices, or just find out about them?

sources.claim: Libet (1983): readiness potential ~500 ms before movement, conscious urge ~200 ms before, ~300 ms gap; Libet proposed a conscious veto; Schurger et al. (2012) proposed spontaneous neural fluctuations

publish.title: Does Your Brain Decide Before You Do? 🧠⏱️
publish.description: Libet's famous experiment found brain activity 300 ms before people felt they chose. But is it really decision?
